---
title: "Missing Values"
subtitle: "≈ `NA` · `is.na()` · `replace_na()` · `fill()` · `complete()`"
jupyter: python3
---

R has one missing marker, `NA`, and treats `NaN` as a kind of `NA`. Polars has
two unrelated things: **null**, a missing value in any dtype, and **`NaN`**, an
ordinary float value. Null tools ignore `NaN`, and aggregations skip nulls
without being asked. This chapter covers how each one arises and propagates,
how to count, fill and drop them, and how to find rows that are missing
entirely.

## In tidyverse {#sec-na-tidyverse}

```r
library(tidyverse)

x <- c(1, NA, 0 / 0)          # NA and NaN in one double vector
is.na(x)                      # FALSE TRUE TRUE: NaN counts as missing
mean(x)                       # NA: R makes you decide
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)         # 1: na.rm drops NA *and* NaN

df |> mutate(y = replace_na(y, 0), z = na_if(z, -999), w = coalesce(a, b))
df |> group_by(id) |> fill(dose, .direction = "down")
stocks |> complete(year, qtr)                        # implicit → explicit
flights |> distinct(tailnum) |> anti_join(planes)    # find implicit gaps
```

R's rule: missingness is contagious. Arithmetic, comparisons and summaries all
return `NA` until you opt out with `na.rm = TRUE`. Polars keeps contagion for
element-wise operations but **not** for aggregations, and it never treats `NaN`
as missing.

## Mental model {#sec-na-model}

```text
  A Float64 column holding [1.0, null, NaN]

  values   │ 1.0 │  ·  │ NaN │
  validity │  1  │  0  │  1  │      null = validity bit 0; NaN = a valid float value

                  null                                  NaN
  dtypes          every dtype                           Float16 / Float32 / Float64 only
  comes from      None, empty CSV field, failed cast,   0/0, sqrt(-1), log(-1),
                  shift(), outer joins, pivot gaps      "NaN" in a CSV float column
  detect          is_null()                             is_nan()       (null → null)
  aggregations    skipped                               propagate: mean, sum → NaN
  equality        null == null → null                   NaN == NaN → true
  R analog        NA                                    NaN, but R's is.na(NaN) is TRUE
```

The validity bit is explained in [Data Model](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-model).
Each tool family sees only its own kind:

| Task | null | `NaN` |
|---|---|---|
| detect | `is_null()`, `is_not_null()` | `is_nan()`, `is_not_nan()` |
| count | `null_count()` | `is_nan().sum()` |
| replace | `fill_null()` | `fill_nan()` |
| drop rows | `drop_nulls()` | `drop_nans()` |
| convert | — | `fill_nan(None)` turns `NaN` into null |

: Two markers, two tool families {.striped}

## Mechanics {#sec-na-mechanics}

```{python}
#| include: false
%xmode Minimal
```

```{python}
import datetime as dt

import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs
from pl_notes import datasets

penguins_df = datasets.penguins()
flights_df = datasets.flights()
weather_df = datasets.weather()
planes_df = datasets.planes()
airports_df = datasets.airports()
```

### Null vs NaN {#sec-na-nan}

`NaN` comes from float arithmetic that has no answer. Null comes from missing
input, and passes through arithmetic as null:

```{python}
ratio_df = pl.DataFrame({"num": [0.0, -1.0, 1.0, None], "den": [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0]})

ratio_df.with_columns(
    ratio=pl.col("num") / pl.col("den"),
    sqrt=pl.col("num").sqrt(),
).with_columns(
    is_null=pl.col("ratio").is_null(),
    is_nan=pl.col("ratio").is_nan(),
)
```

`1 / 0` is `inf`, not `NaN`. `is_nan()` of a null is null, not `false`.
Integer `//` and `%` by zero give null rather than an error.

In a CSV, an empty field is null, and the string `NaN` in a float column
parses as `NaN`. Unlike readr (default `na = c("", "NA")`), Polars does not
read `NA` as missing unless you pass `null_values="NA"`, which is what
`pl_notes.datasets` does:

```{python}
pl.read_csv(b"reading,site\n1.5,A\nNaN,NA\n,B\n")
```

**A realistic `NaN`.** Each hour's share of the day's rainfall is
`precip / daily total`. On a dry day that is `0 / 0`:

```{python}
weather_df_share = weather_df.with_columns(
    precip_share=pl.col("precip") / pl.col("precip").sum().over("origin", "month", "day")
)

weather_df_share.select(
    null_count=pl.col("precip_share").null_count(),
    nan_count=pl.col("precip_share").is_nan().sum(),
    mean=pl.col("precip_share").mean(),
    mean_rainy=pl.col("precip_share").fill_nan(None).mean(),
)
```

Two thirds of the column is `NaN`, `null_count()` reports zero, and one `NaN`
poisons the mean. `fill_nan(None)` converts `NaN` to null, after which `mean()`
skips them. In R, `is.na()` and `na.rm = TRUE` would have handled both.

**`NaN` is a value with a place in the order.** Polars treats `NaN` as equal to
itself and greater than `inf`, so it sorts and groups predictably. `max()`
skips it, though, while `mean()` propagates it:

```{python}
x = pl.Series("x", [3.0, float("nan"), float("inf"), None, 1.0])
{
    "x == x": (x == x).to_list(),
    "sort()": x.sort().to_list(),
    "max(), nan_max()": (x.max(), x.nan_max()),
    "mean()": x.mean(),
    "n_unique()": x.n_unique(),
}
```

In R, `NaN == NaN` is `NA`, `sort()` drops `NaN`, and `max(c(1, NaN))` is
`NaN`.

### How nulls propagate {#sec-na-propagation}

Every row below was verified on Polars 2.0. `x` is a column with nulls.

| Operation | Polars | R |
|---|---|---|
| `x + 1`, `x * 0`, `x ** 0` | null | `NA`, `NA`, but `NA^0` is `1` |
| `x > 1`, `x == x` | null | `NA` |
| `x.eq_missing(y)`, `x.ne_missing(y)` | null == null → `true`, never null | — |
| `null & False`, `null | True` | `false`, `true` (Kleene logic) | same |
| `null & True`, `null | False`, `~null` | null | same |
| `x.sum()` | skips nulls; all-null → `0` | `sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)`; all-`NA` → `0` |
| `x.mean()`, `median()`, `std()` | skip nulls; all-null → null | `mean(NA, na.rm = TRUE)` → `NaN` |
| `x.min()`, `x.max()` | skip nulls; all-null → null | `max(NA, na.rm = TRUE)` → `-Inf` + warning |
| `x.count()` / `x.len()` | non-null rows / all rows | `sum(!is.na(x))` / `n()` |
| `x.n_unique()`, `unique()`, `group_by()` keys | null is one value, its own group | same |
| `x.first()` | the first row, even if null; `ignore_nulls=True` skips | `first(x, na_rm = TRUE)` |
| `x.cum_sum()` | null stays null, the sum carries on after it | `cumsum()` is `NA` from there on |
| `x.any()`, `x.all()` | skip nulls (`ignore_nulls=True` default) | Kleene: `any(c(FALSE, NA))` → `NA`, `any(c(TRUE, NA))` → `TRUE` |
| `pl.any_horizontal()`, `pl.all_horizontal()` | Kleene logic, like `|` and `&` | `x | y`, `x & y` |
| `pl.sum_horizontal()` | skips nulls; all-null → `0` | `rowSums(na.rm = TRUE)` |
| `x.is_in(["a", None])` | null → null; `nulls_equal=True` → `true` | `NA %in% c("a", NA)` → `TRUE` |
| `x.str.*` | null → null | same |
| `pl.concat_str()` | any null input → null; `ignore_nulls=True` | `str_c()` → `NA`; `paste()` → `"NA"` |
| `when(cond)` with null `cond` | falls through to `otherwise()` | `case_when()`: to `.default`; `if_else()`: `NA` |
| `filter(cond)` with null `cond` | row dropped | same |
| `sort()` | nulls **first**, in both directions | `arrange()`: `NA` last |
| `join()` keys | null never matches null; `nulls_equal=True` | `na_matches = "na"`: `NA` matches `NA` |

: Null propagation, operation by operation {.striped}

**Kleene logic** treats null as "true or false, unknown". `null & False` is
`false` whatever the unknown is, so the answer is known. R does exactly the
same, so this is one place where R intuition is right:

```{python}
bool_df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [True, False, None]}, schema={"a": pl.Boolean})

bool_df.join(bool_df.rename({"a": "b"}), how="cross").with_columns(
    a_and_b=pl.col("a") & pl.col("b"),
    a_or_b=pl.col("a") | pl.col("b"),
    not_a=~pl.col("a"),
).filter(pl.col("a").is_null()).sort("b", descending=True, nulls_last=True)
```

**Aggregations** on a column with one null and on a column with only nulls:

```{python}
agg_df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"some_null": [1, None, 3], "all_null": [None, None, None]},
    schema={"some_null": pl.Int64, "all_null": pl.Int64},
)
aggs = {
    "sum": pl.all().sum(), "mean": pl.all().mean(), "max": pl.all().max(),
    "first": pl.all().first(), "count": pl.all().count(), "len": pl.all().len(),
    "n_unique": pl.all().n_unique(), "null_count": pl.all().null_count(),
}
pl.concat(   # one row per aggregation; cast to String so the rows stack
    agg_df.select(pl.lit(name).alias("agg"), expr.cast(pl.String))
    for name, expr in aggs.items()
)
```

`sum()` of nothing is `0` (as in R with `na.rm = TRUE`), but `mean()` and
`max()` of nothing are null, where R returns `NaN` and `-Inf`. `n_unique()`
counts null as a value.

**Element-wise functions** keep nulls in place, with two exceptions worth
knowing: `cum_sum()` carries on after a null, and `is_in()` returns null for a
null input:

```{python}
toy_df = pl.DataFrame({"n": [1, None, 3], "s": ["a", None, "c"], "t": ["A", "B", None]})

toy_df.with_columns(
    cum_sum=pl.col("n").cum_sum(),
    is_in=pl.col("s").is_in(["a", None]),
    is_in_eq=pl.col("s").is_in(["a", None], nulls_equal=True),
    concat=pl.concat_str("s", "t", separator="-"),
    concat_skip=pl.concat_str("s", "t", separator="-", ignore_nulls=True),
)
```

**`when/then`** treats a null condition as not true, so the row gets the
`otherwise()` value. The two penguins with no body mass become "light":

```{python}
penguins_df.with_columns(
    size=pl.when(pl.col("body_mass_g") > 4000).then(pl.lit("heavy")).otherwise(pl.lit("light")),
).filter(pl.col("body_mass_g").is_null()).select("species", "body_mass_g", "size")
```

`if_else(body_mass_g > 4000, "heavy", "light")` would give `NA`. Test
`.is_null()` in the first branch if you need a separate label.

**Joins** never match null keys, but they do match `NaN` keys, because `NaN`
is a value (more in [Joins](../transform/joins.qmd)):

```{python}
left_df = pl.DataFrame({"key": [1.0, float("nan"), None], "left": ["a", "b", "c"]})
right_df = pl.DataFrame({"key": [1.0, float("nan"), None], "right": ["x", "y", "z"]})

left_df.join(right_df, on="key", how="inner")
```

`nulls_equal=True` adds the third row. dplyr matches `NA` to `NA` by default.

### Counting and diagnosing {#sec-na-counting}

`null_count()` on a frame is `colSums(is.na(df))`; a long, sorted version with
percentages is in @sec-na-recipes. Per row, sum the `is_null()` flags
horizontally (≈ `rowSums(is.na(df))`). Two penguins are missing every
measurement and `sex`, and nine more are missing only `sex`:

```{python}
penguins_df.with_columns(n_missing=pl.sum_horizontal(pl.all().is_null())).group_by(
    "n_missing"
).len().sort("n_missing")
```

Also available: `has_nulls()` (a Boolean per column), `df.count()` (non-null
counts), and `df.describe()`, which includes a `null_count` row. Missingness
often has structure; the `flights` example is in @sec-na-mean-trap.

### Filling {#sec-na-filling}

`fill_null()` takes a value, an expression, or a `strategy=`:

```{python}
dose = pl.Series("dose", [None, 1, None, None, 4, None])

pl.DataFrame(dose).with_columns(
    forward=pl.col("dose").fill_null(strategy="forward"),           # tidyr fill() "down"
    forward_1=pl.col("dose").fill_null(strategy="forward", limit=1),
    backward=pl.col("dose").fill_null(strategy="backward"),         # "up"
    mean=pl.col("dose").fill_null(strategy="mean"),
    zero=pl.col("dose").fill_null(strategy="zero"),
    linear=pl.col("dose").interpolate(),
)
```

The strategies are `"forward"`, `"backward"`, `"min"`, `"max"`, `"mean"`,
`"zero"` and `"one"`. `limit=` caps how many consecutive nulls a forward or
backward fill crosses. Leading and trailing nulls stay null when there is
nothing to carry. Note that `mean` is `2`, not `2.5`: see @sec-na-fill-dtype.

**Fill within groups** (≈ `group_by(patient) |> fill(dose_mg)`). Forward
filling follows row order, so if rows are not in time order, pass `order_by=`:

```{python}
visits_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "patient": ["A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B"],
    "day": [1, 1, 3, 2, 2, 3],
    "dose_mg": [10, None, None, 5, 20, None],
})

visits_df.with_columns(
    by_row=pl.col("dose_mg").fill_null(strategy="forward").over("patient"),
    by_day=pl.col("dose_mg").fill_null(strategy="forward").over("patient", order_by="day"),
)
```

Patient A's day 3 is the third row. Filled in row order it takes day 1's
`10`; filled in day order it takes day 2's `20`. Patient B's day 1 stays null
because there is nothing before it.

**Fill from another column** with `pl.coalesce()` (≈ `coalesce()`). The peak
wind is the gust when one was recorded, otherwise the sustained speed:

```{python}
weather_df.select(
    "origin", "time_hour", "wind_speed", "wind_gust",
    peak_wind=pl.coalesce("wind_gust", "wind_speed"),
).head(3)
```

`pl.coalesce("a", "b", 0)` adds a final constant. Bare strings are column
names here; use `pl.lit()` for a string value (see
[Expressions](../core/expressions.qmd#sec-expr-literals)).

**Interpolate.** `interpolate()` assumes equally spaced rows (≈
`zoo::na.approx()`). `interpolate_by()` uses an actual x axis, such as a
time column:

```{python}
readings_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "hour": [0, 1, 4, 5],
    "temp": [10.0, None, None, 15.0],
})

readings_df.with_columns(
    by_row=pl.col("temp").interpolate(),
    by_hour=pl.col("temp").interpolate_by("hour"),
)
```

`interpolate()` returns `Float64` even for an integer column, and it fills
nulls only; `NaN` stays `NaN`.

### Value → null, and dropping {#sec-na-dropping}

Sentinel codes such as `-999` and `""` become null with `replace(old, None)`
(≈ `na_if()`). `old` may be a list, and with selectors one call cleans many
columns:

```{python}
survey_df_raw = pl.DataFrame({
    "id": [1, 2, 3],
    "temp": [21.5, -999.0, 22.1],
    "count": [5, 7, -999],
    "site": ["A", "", "N/A"],
})

survey_df_clean = survey_df_raw.with_columns(
    cs.numeric().replace(-999, None),
    cs.string().replace(["", "N/A"], None),
)
survey_df_clean
```

The dtypes are unchanged. To drop rows, `drop_nulls()` checks every column and
`subset=` limits it (≈ `drop_na(body_mass_g)`); `drop_nans()` is the `NaN`
twin and keeps nulls:

```{python}
{
    "rows": penguins_df.height,
    "drop_nulls()": penguins_df.drop_nulls().height,
    "drop_nulls(subset='body_mass_g')": penguins_df.drop_nulls(subset="body_mass_g").height,
    "drop_nans() on precip_share": weather_df_share.drop_nans().height,
}
```

### Explicit vs implicit missing {#sec-na-implicit}

R4DS separates two kinds of missing data. An **explicit** missing value is a
null in a row that exists. An **implicit** missing value is a row that should
exist but doesn't. Every tool so far only sees explicit nulls.

```text
 stocks (7 rows)              pivot(on="qtr")                complete(year, qtr)
 year qtr price               year   1     2     3     4     2020 4 null  ← explicit
 2020  4  null  ← explicit    2020  1.88  0.59  0.35  null   2021 1 null  ← was implicit
 (2021 Q1 has no row)         2021  null  0.92  0.17  2.66
```

`complete()` is a cross join of the key values plus a left join back. A flag
column added before the join records which rows were observed, so the two kinds
stay distinguishable afterwards:

```{python}
stocks_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "year": [2020, 2020, 2020, 2020, 2021, 2021, 2021],
    "qtr": [1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 3, 4],
    "price": [1.88, 0.59, 0.35, None, 0.92, 0.17, 2.66],
})

stocks_df_complete = (
    stocks_df.select("year").unique()
    .join(stocks_df.select("qtr").unique(), how="cross")
    .join(stocks_df.with_columns(observed=pl.lit(True)), on=["year", "qtr"], how="left")
    .sort("year", "qtr")
)
stocks_df_complete.filter(pl.col("price").is_null())
```

The reverse, explicit → implicit, is `drop_nulls()` (≈ `pivot_longer(...,
values_drop_na = TRUE)`). Pivoting is covered in
[Reshaping](../transform/reshape.qmd).

**Find the gaps with an anti-join.** `weather` should have one row per airport
per hour of 2013. `complete()` only knows values that appear somewhere, so a
full calendar has to come from outside the data (≈ `full_seq()`):

```{python}
hours_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "time_hour": pl.datetime_range(
        dt.datetime(2013, 1, 1), dt.datetime(2013, 12, 31, 23),
        interval="1h", time_zone="America/New_York", eager=True,
    )
})
weather_grid_df = weather_df.select("origin").unique().join(hours_df, how="cross")

weather_df_gaps = weather_grid_df.join(weather_df, on=["origin", "time_hour"], how="anti")
weather_df_gaps.group_by("origin").len().sort("origin")
```

That is 165 missing station-hours. At every station the data starts at 01:00
on 1 January and ends at 18:00 on 30 December, so 30 of each station's gaps
sit at the edges of the year. To fill the gaps, make them explicit with a left
join, then interpolate along time within each station:

```{python}
weather_df_hourly = (
    weather_grid_df.join(weather_df, on=["origin", "time_hour"], how="left")
    .sort("origin", "time_hour")
    .with_columns(temp_filled=pl.col("temp").interpolate_by("time_hour").over("origin"))
)
weather_df_hourly.select(
    temp_nulls=pl.col("temp").null_count(),
    temp_filled_nulls=pl.col("temp_filled").null_count(),
)
```

`temp` now has 166 nulls: the 165 new rows plus one that was already explicit.
The 90 left after interpolating are those 30 edge hours per station, because
interpolation needs a value on both sides.

**Keys in one table, missing from another.** The R4DS examples translate
directly. Four destinations are missing from `airports`, and 722 tail numbers
(one of them null) are missing from `planes`:

```{python}
{
    "dest not in airports": flights_df.select("dest").unique()
    .join(airports_df, left_on="dest", right_on="faa", how="anti")
    .sort("dest")["dest"].to_list(),
    "tailnum not in planes": flights_df.select("tailnum").unique()
    .join(planes_df, on="tailnum", how="anti").height,
}
```

The null tail number shows up because a null key matches nothing. In this
case dplyr gives the same count, since `planes` has no `NA` key to match.

**Empty groups** are implicit missing rows too. `group_by()` on an `Enum`
returns only the levels that occur (there is no `.drop = FALSE`); to keep the
others, left-join the summary onto a frame of all levels, built from
`dtype.categories`.

## Where it bites {#sec-na-gotchas}

| R behaviour | Polars behaviour |
|---|---|
| `is.na(NaN)` is `TRUE`; `na.rm` drops `NaN` | `NaN` is not null; null tools ignore it (@sec-na-nan) |
| `mean(x)` with an `NA` → `NA` | `mean()` skips nulls silently |
| `filter(x)` and `filter(!x)` both drop `NA` rows | the same with `~`: null rows are in neither half |
| `replace_na()` refuses the wrong type | `fill_null()` can change the dtype |
| `any(c(FALSE, NA))` → `NA` | `.any()` → `false`, but `any_horizontal()` → null |

: Traps at a glance (the rest are in the propagation table, @sec-na-propagation) {.striped}

Kleene `&` and `|` and nulls forming their own group are also the same in
both languages.

### `mean()` hides how many rows it used {#sec-na-mean-trap}

R's `NA` result forces a decision. Polars just answers, so check `count()`
against `len()` when the nulls carry meaning. In `flights`, a null `dep_time`
means a cancelled flight:

```{python}
flights_df.select(
    n=pl.len(),
    cancelled=pl.col("dep_time").is_null().sum(),
    n_used=pl.col("arr_delay").count(),
    mean_arr_delay=pl.col("arr_delay").mean(),
)
```

The mean uses 327,346 of 336,776 flights. It silently drops the 8,255
cancellations and 1,175 more flights that departed but have no recorded
arrival delay.

### A filter and its negation don't cover all rows {#sec-na-filter-trap}

`filter()` drops rows where the condition is null, and `~null` is still null.
The two penguins with no body mass are in neither half:

```{python}
heavy = pl.col("body_mass_g") > 4000
{
    "heavy": penguins_df.filter(heavy).height,
    "~heavy": penguins_df.filter(~heavy).height,
    "total": penguins_df.height,
}
```

dplyr's `filter()` behaves the same. To keep them, write the complement
explicitly: `~heavy | pl.col("body_mass_g").is_null()`. Similarly,
`filter(pl.col("x").is_not_nan())` drops nulls as well as `NaN`, because
`is_not_nan()` of a null is null; `drop_nans()` keeps them.

### `fill_null()` and dtypes {#sec-na-fill-dtype}

`replace_na()` refuses a value of the wrong type. `fill_null()` on an
expression finds a common dtype instead:

```{python}
int_df = pl.DataFrame({"n": [1, 4, None], "s": ["a", "b", None]})

int_df.with_columns(
    mean_strategy=pl.col("n").fill_null(strategy="mean"),   # Int64: 2.5 truncated to 2
    mean_expr=pl.col("n").fill_null(pl.col("n").mean()),     # Float64: 2.5
    n_as_text=pl.col("n").fill_null("missing"),              # Int64 becomes String
)
```

The frame-level `int_df.fill_null(0)` behaves differently again: it fills only
the columns whose dtype fits the value (`n`, not `s`), so
`df.fill_null(0)` is a safe "numeric columns only" shortcut.

### `.any()` and `any_horizontal()` disagree {#sec-na-any-trap}

Column-wise `.any()` and `.all()` skip nulls by default; the row-wise versions
use Kleene logic. With `b` all null:

```{python}
flags_df = pl.DataFrame(
    {"a": [False, True], "b": [None, None]}, schema={"a": pl.Boolean, "b": pl.Boolean}
)
flags_df.with_columns(
    b_any=pl.col("b").any(),                           # nulls skipped → false
    b_any_kleene=pl.col("b").any(ignore_nulls=False),  # R's any(c(NA, NA)) → NA
    a_or_b=pl.any_horizontal("a", "b"),                # false | null → null
)
```

## Recipes {#sec-na-recipes}

**Missingness summary per column**, long and sorted (≈ `naniar::miss_var_summary()`):

```{python}
weather_df.null_count().unpivot(variable_name="column", value_name="n_missing").with_columns(
    pct_missing=(pl.col("n_missing") / weather_df.height * 100).round(1)
).filter(pl.col("n_missing") > 0).sort("n_missing", descending=True)
```

**Cancelled flights by scheduled hour** (R4DS: `mean(is.na(dep_time))`). The
mean of a Boolean is the share of `true`:

```{python}
flights_df.group_by(hour=pl.col("sched_dep_time") // 100).agg(
    n=pl.len(),
    prop_cancelled=pl.col("dep_time").is_null().mean(),
    mean_dep_delay=pl.col("dep_delay").mean(),
).filter(pl.col("hour") > 1).sort("prop_cancelled", descending=True).head(4)
```

`mean_dep_delay` covers only the flights that left, because nulls are skipped.

**Flag before you fill**, so imputed values stay identifiable:

```{python}
penguins_df.with_columns(
    mass_imputed=pl.col("body_mass_g").is_null(),
    body_mass_g=pl.col("body_mass_g").fill_null(pl.col("body_mass_g").mean().over("species")),
).filter(pl.col("mass_imputed")).select("species", "body_mass_g", "mass_imputed")
```

Both expressions read the original column, because expressions in one context
run in parallel ([Expressions](../core/expressions.qmd#sec-expr-parallel)).
